item.statement: Ketamine trip reports read more like near-death accounts than those for any other drug.
item.why: In one study, a computer compared the words in about 15,000 online reports on 165 drugs with 625 near-death accounts, and ketamine's came out closest, with salvia and LSD close behind. Only words were compared, though: nobody showed the experiences themselves feel alike.

quiz.reason: Trick: the study did find ketamine reports read most like near-death accounts, of 165 drugs, yet the card calls it a myth on 'words, not feelings', and its why never states that finding. Rewritten as the true finding, with the words-only limit kept.

item.statement: Kids who had the original DARE classes used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs less than kids who didn't.
item.why: Across 11 studies, kids who had the original classes said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't. DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that newer version wasn't part of this review.

quiz.reason: Weak as written: a scope caveat padded with dates and sample sizes, not something forum readers argue about. Rebuilt on the finding they do repeat (no difference with DARE), keeping 'original' in the statement and the 2001 rebuild in the why so the verdict does not cover the new version. If a card on that finding already exists, drop this one as weak.

item.statement: Headaches from skipping caffeine come from expecting them, not from the missing caffeine.
item.why: Off their usual caffeine before a small operation, 10 of 20 people on dummy pills had a headache by evening and none of 20 on caffeine pills did, and neither they nor the doctor checking knew who got which. Only 40 patients took part, though, and surgery can also cause headaches.

quiz.reason: Form: the why led with the method and buried the result in a long second sentence. Same facts, result first.

item.statement: A trial showed psilocybin works better than an antidepressant for depression.
item.why: In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression at 6 weeks or 6 months, even though people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin. But the trial was too small to show the two work equally well.

quiz.reason: The statement is a side detail most readers would guess right (higher hopes for psilocybin); what people argue about is whether psilocybin beat the antidepressant. Reframed on that ('Not shown' in the lines), with the expectation gap kept in the why.
Note: the lines say only 'the medicine'; the names clonidine and lofexidine rest on the answer's question, so editors may want to confirm the three trials cover both.

item.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.
item.why: In one study of ten healthy people, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self on the S form, while on the R form they described relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug, though.

quiz.reason: Certainty: 'the R form brought relaxation' turns a report into an effect; the lines say people described relaxation. Reworded only.
